thread.title: Tech Today: Apple HomePod a Dud, Nice PC Numbers, Zuck’s Mixed Reviews - Barron's

author: Tiernan Ray
title: Tech Today: Apple HomePod a Dud, Nice PC Numbers, Zuck’s Mixed Reviews - Barron's
text:
By Tiernan Ray Updated April 12, 2018 10:23 a.m. ET Here are some things going on today in the world of tech :
Apple HomePod fizzles Apple ’s ( AAPL ) HomePod smart speaker is a dud, according to Bloomberg ’s Mark Gurman , who writes today that the company has lowered its sales forecasts for the device and cut orders for parts, citing an unnamed source.
During the first 10 weeks of sales, the HomePod got just 10% of the smart speaker category’s sales, versus 73% for Amazon.com ’s (AMZN) Echo devices, writes Gurman, and 14% for Alphabet ’s ( GOOGL ) Google Home speaker.
Apple shares today are up $2.06, or 1.2%, at $174.50.
Cheers for ‘stable’ PC market The Street is perusing those personal computer shipment data for Q1 that came out after the closing bell yesterday.
David Wong with Wells Fargo calls the results "fairly good,” prompting him to reiterate his Outperform ratings on Intel ( INTC ), Advanced Micro Devices ( AMD ), and Micron Technology ( MU ).
Wong thinks the good times could roll into this quarter, given a raft of new processors introduced by Intel and AMD, including the first of AMD’s chips that have an “integrated” GPU , or graphics circuitry, called “Vega”; and Intel’s microprocessors called "Kaby Lake” that include that same Vega GPU circuitry through a partnership with AMD, as well as Intel’s new versions of "Coffee Lake” chips for desktops and notebooks.
Intel shares are up $1.22, or 2.4%, at $52.32, while AMD stock is up 22 cents, or 2%, at $10.04.
Good news for Microsoft Michael Nemeroff of Credit Suisse , who follows Microsoft ( MSFT ), is encouraged by the report, noting that there is a “high correlation” between PC sales and when a company upgrades its productivity suite software, i.e., Office . That’s encouraging for the subscription version Microsoft offers, Office 365 .
However, Nemeroff, who has an Outperform rating on Microsoft, is less interested in the PC trends when looking out in time, because he expects “Windows-related revenue will decline” for the company, to perhaps just 15% of the company’s revenue next year and just 10% by 2020.
Microsoft shares are up $1.74, or 1.9%, at $93.60.
Zuck’s still positive reviews Following a second day of testimony before Congress by Facebook ( FB ) CEO Mark Zuckerberg , the stock is down $1.77, or 1%, at $164.55.
Facebook CEO Mark Zuckerberg Illustration: Getty Images Among reviews today from the Street, Cowen & Co .’s John Blackledge reiterates an Outperform rating, writing that "Zuckerberg did well under Congressional scrutiny in our view, and while political/reg. hurdles likely persist, FB is open to working together to solve the issues."
He notes that his own survey conducted among 2,500 people using Facebook found that time spent on the property “declined moderately in Q1,” which was a result, it would seem, not of bad sentiment but of changes that the company made to the platform during the quarter.
Not everyone is satisfied.
Brian Weiser with Pivotal Research , who rates Facebook shares a Sell, expects more bad headlines for the company. Today he writes,
“Indications that the US Congress will investigate Cambridge Analytica, upcoming testimony from Facebook in the UK parliament—which unwisely for Facebook will not include its CEO—and the looming implementation of GDPR in Europe next month suggest more negative regulatory newsflow to come.
"And that’s before considering the high likelihood that additional data leaks will be acknowledged and that other operational problems will come to light."
My colleague Jon Swartz has more on the Street reaction .
Little sense in a chip trade war Bernstein analysts Stacy Rasgon, Mark Li, and Mark Newman consider the implications of tariffs on the semiconductor and technology industry generally, after acknowledging that they’ve been getting questions from clients about the matter.
They conclude there’s little sense in a trade war over tech. Out of $50 billion of U.S. exports of chips to the world, only about $6 billion was exported to China, write the analysts.
The U.S. has put tariffs on some “discrete” imports, they note, like individual transistors , but "a larger trade war with China on semis makes little sense,” they conclude.
"Escalation is the larger worry,” the analysts write,” as most semis are "imported" to the U.S. from China inside "semi-rich" end products (smartphones, computers, and other electronic goods that, except for a few TVs, have so far been mostly spared).
